questions.stem: A pregnant patient is not immune to rubella. When should she get the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine?
questions.explanation: D is correct: MMR is a live vaccine, so it is not given in pregnancy; give it after delivery, before discharge. A and B give a live vaccine during pregnancy. C misses the chance to protect her after delivery.

questions.stem: Which vaccines are live? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: A, C, D, and E are correct: MMR, varicella, the nasal flu spray, and yellow fever are live. B, Shingrix, is not live. F, the injected flu shot, is inactivated.

questions.stem: A patient on high-dose steroids asks for the nasal flu spray. What is the best action?

options.text: Give the injected flu shot instead

questions.explanation: A is correct: the nasal spray is live, so avoid it in immunosuppressed patients; the injected flu shot is inactivated and recommended. B and D give a live vaccine to an immunosuppressed patient. C leaves the patient without protection when a safe vaccine exists.

questions.stem: A patient got the MMR vaccine 14 days ago. Today they get the varicella vaccine. What is the best plan?

options.text: Repeat the varicella vaccine at least 28 days after it was given

questions.explanation: B is correct: two live injected vaccines go on the same day or at least 28 days apart; 14 days is too close, so the second one may not work and is repeated. A ignores the spacing rule. C repeats the wrong vaccine. D is still too close.

questions.stem: After the MMR vaccine, how long should a patient avoid getting pregnant?
questions.explanation: D is correct: after the vaccine, avoid getting pregnant for 4 weeks. A is too short. C is longer than taught. B ignores the rule for this live vaccine.

questions.stem: Which statement about Shingrix is correct?

options.text: It is not live, so it can be used in many immunocompromised adults

questions.explanation: B is correct: Shingrix is not live, so it can be used in many immunocompromised adults. A is wrong because it is not live. C is wrong because it is 2 doses. D is wrong because it starts at 50.

questions.stem: A healthy 52-year-old has never had a pneumococcal vaccine. What is recommended?

options.text: Only if they have lung disease

questions.explanation: A is correct: pneumococcal vaccine is for all adults 50 and older. B uses an older age cutoff. C limits it to a risk group, but at 50 and older it is for everyone. D ignores the recommendation.

questions.stem: A healthy 68-year-old with no risk factors asks about the respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) vaccine. What fits the schedule taught?

options.text: Recommended at 75, or at 50 to 74 if at higher risk

questions.explanation: D is correct: RSV vaccine is for everyone 75 and older and for ages 50 to 74 at higher risk, as one dose. A is wrong because this patient has no risk factors and is under 75. C is wrong because it is one dose. B is wrong because adults are included.

questions.stem: When should the tetanus, diphtheria, and whooping cough booster (Tdap) be given in pregnancy?
questions.explanation: A is correct: give the booster in every pregnancy. B misses later pregnancies. C and D skip it during pregnancy, when it is recommended.

questions.stem: Which statements about live and inactivated vaccines are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Live vaccines are avoided in pregnancy
Live vaccines are avoided in people with weak immune systems
Inactivated vaccines can be given any time relative to other vaccines
Two live vaccines must be 6 months apart

questions.explanation: A, B, and C are correct: live vaccines are avoided in pregnancy and weak immune systems, and inactivated vaccines can be given any time. D is wrong because two live vaccines go the same day or at least 28 days apart. E is wrong because Shingrix is not live.
